company.title: Blockbuster (1985–2010): debt, late fees and Netflix
company.description: Blockbuster ended 2004 with 9,094 stores, borrowed heavily to leave Viacom and gave up late fees. It filed for bankruptcy in 2010; one franchised store remains.

card.blurb: The biggest name in home video had 9,094 stores in 2004, a billion dollars of new debt and a rival it had declined to buy. One franchised store in Oregon still rents films under the sign.

hero.dates: First store opened Oct 19, 1985. Filed for Chapter 11 on Sep 23, 2010.
hero.standfirst: It had a store within a short drive of most American homes. Then the drive stopped being necessary.
hero.deck: Blockbuster was the [video rental chain](/category/film/) that ended 2004 with 9,094 stores in 25 countries and filed for bankruptcy in 2010. Its 2004 revenue was just over $6 billion. That year it borrowed heavily to pay a parting distribution as it left its parent, Viacom, and prepared to give up the late fees that had carried its profits.

findings.title: The stores did not empty overnight.
findings.text: Revenue was still $5.07B in 2008, four years after the peak. What collapsed first was profit: the company reported a net loss in every year from 1997 to 2010 except 2006.[^2][^6][^9][^10]

findings.title: It left Viacom carrying debt.
findings.text: Long-term debt went from $75.1M at the end of 2003 to $1,119.7M a year later, after a $1.15B credit facility and $300M of notes paid for a $5.00 a share distribution on the way out.[^5][^6]

findings.title: Late fees were a pillar, and it knocked the pillar out.
findings.text: Extended viewing fees were $692.6M in 1999, or 15.5% of revenue. Ending them in 2005 was expected to cost $250M to $300M of operating income a year.[^2][^5]

findings.title: It had a credible answer to Netflix, late.
findings.text: Blockbuster Online launched in August 2004 and reached about 2.2 million subscribers by the end of 2006. Netflix had 6.3 million by then.[^5][^7][^21]

findings.title: The name outlived everything else.
findings.text: Dish closed the corporate stores by January 2014. Franchisees carried on, and since 2019 the Bend store has been the only one in the world.[^27][^29][^30]

items.title: The Bend store
items.text: A franchise at 211 NE Revere Avenue in Bend, Oregon, owned by Ken and Debbie Tisher and managed by Sandi Harding. It opened in 1992 as Pacific Video, became a Blockbuster in 2000, and has been the only one in the world since 2019.[^29][^30] Its website was live on October 3, 2026, with current releases and merchandise.[^31]

items.title: The brand
items.text: Dish Network bought it with the rest of the assets in 2011 and used it for a streaming package, Blockbuster@Home.[^13][^28] Dish became part of EchoStar on December 31, 2023.[^36] On October 3, 2026 blockbuster.com showed the logo, the line “We are working on rewinding your movie” and a link to Sling TV.[^32]

items.title: The corporate stores
items.text: About 300 were left when Dish announced the end on November 6, 2013. They were to close by early January 2014, with about 2,800 jobs lost.[^27] The Mexican business was sold on January 14, 2014.[^28]

items.title: The shareholders
items.text: The company said it expected no proceeds from the sale to be available to preferred or common stockholders and that all classes of stock would be canceled.[^13]

items.title: The management
items.text: James Keyes and three other senior executives were terminated on April 26, 2011, the day the sale closed.[^13] John Antioco wrote in 2011 that he now invests in retail franchise concepts.[^19]

items.title: The rival it did not buy
items.text: Netflix reported revenue of $45.18B for 2025.[^23]

now.title: The BLOCKBUSTER word mark
now.text: The USPTO lists two live registrations for the word mark, 1771243 (renewed, status date Nov. 3, 2023) and 3661761 (renewed, status date Jul. 26, 2019). Blockbuster L.L.C., a Colorado limited liability company in Englewood, is the owner of record. The registration for the torn-ticket logo, 5008368, was cancelled on Feb. 10, 2023 because the registrant did not file an acceptable declaration under Section 8. We checked these three records only.

now.title: The name inside Dish
now.text: At the end of 2013 Dish used the name for Blockbuster@Home, which its FY2013 10-K describes as giving Dish subscribers streaming access to more than 10,000 movies and TV shows. We do not know whether it still exists. EchoStar completed its acquisition of Dish on December 31, 2023. On October 10, 2026 blockbuster.com showed a holding page that says the company is working on rewinding your movie, with a link to Sling TV. We found no source that names the parent of Blockbuster L.L.C. today.

now.title: The estate
now.text: Blockbuster’s Chapter 11 case number, 10-14997, appears in CourtListener’s record under the caption BB Liquidating Inc. The record lists the case as Chapter 7 with Robert L. Geltzer as trustee and shows it terminated on June 29, 2017. It is metadata only, so we do not know when the case moved to Chapter 7.

now.title: The Bend store
now.text: A franchise at 211 NE Revere Ave #3, Bend, Oregon, which Seattle Met’s profile lists. The Associated Press reported that Ken and Debbie Tisher have leased the property since 1992, when it was a Pacific Video store, and that it was franchised in 2000 and became a Blockbuster. The Bulletin counted Bend as the only Blockbuster left in the contiguous 48 states in March 2018; the AP dates the Alaska closings to 2018 and the Perth, Australia closing to 2019. In February 2023 the store said movie rentals for locals were up about 200 percent and that some mornings it filled 90 online orders, against a busiest-day figure of 20 the previous February. We could not reach the store’s own website on October 10, 2026, so the latest report we could read is Seattle Met’s.

now.title: The corporate stores
now.text: Dish operated over 1,500 stores in the United States on December 31, 2011 and approximately 800 on December 31, 2012. On November 6, 2013 it announced that about 300 remaining stores would close, expected by early January, with about 2,800 people losing their jobs. Its FY2013 10-K says Blockbuster had ceased all material operations as of December 31, 2013, and gives no date for the last store. Blockbuster UK entered administration on January 16, 2013, and Engadget reported on December 12 that its 91 remaining stores were to close on December 16. Dish completed the sale of Blockbuster Mexico on January 14, 2014. It reported net losses from discontinued operations, which include its Blockbuster businesses, of $47 million for 2013 and $37 million for 2012.

causes.title: The trip to the store stopped being necessary
causes.text: Mail, kiosks and then streaming each removed a reason to drive to a shop. Netflix grew from 857,000 subscribers at the end of 2002 to 20 million at the end of 2010, and [Redbox](/redbox/) had some 30,200 kiosks by then. Blockbuster’s store count fell 41% from its peak over the same years.[^21][^22][^24][^6][^10]

causes.title: Debt taken on to leave Viacom
causes.text: Long-term debt rose from $75.1M to $1,119.7M in 2004, the year of a $905.6M distribution to shareholders. The company went into its fight with Netflix and Redbox owing about a billion dollars, and still owed “nearly $1 billion” when it filed.[^5][^6][^11]

causes.title: A profit model built on late fees
causes.text: Extended viewing fees were $692.6M in 1999. Competitors sold the absence of late fees, and when Blockbuster matched them in 2005 it expected to forgo $250M to $300M of operating income a year.[^2][^4][^5]

causes.title: A late and interrupted response
causes.text: Blockbuster Online launched in August 2004, when Netflix already had 2.6 million subscribers. Total Access took it past 2 million by the end of 2006, but the chief executive who built it left in 2007 after a board fight and a bonus dispute.[^5][^7][^21][^15][^17]

causes.title: Too many leases
causes.text: More than 9,000 stores were an asset while customers came to them and a fixed cost when they did not. The company closed 374 U.S. stores in 2009 alone, and Dish Network later said that too few stores remained to carry the corporate overhead.[^9][^28]

people.title: Who ran it
people.lede: Roles and dates come from [Blockbuster’s filings](#sources) and the accounts cited. A later career appears only where we found a source for it.

people.name: David Cook
people.text: Came from a software business serving the Texas oil industry. Opened the first store in Dallas with some 8,000 tapes and a computerized checkout, and left in 1987 after selling part of the company.[^20]

people.name: Wayne Huizenga
people.text: A founder of Waste Management. His group bought in during 1987, he took control and moved the headquarters to Fort Lauderdale, and the chain grew by acquisition and new openings until the Viacom merger.[^20]

people.name: John F. Antioco
people.text: Took the company public in 1999, ended late fees and launched Blockbuster Online and Total Access. Lost his board seat to Carl Icahn’s slate in May 2005 and was reappointed chairman two days later.[^15][^19][^7]
people.later: Wrote in 2011 that he invests in retail franchise concepts.[^19]

people.name: Carl C. Icahn
people.text: By Antioco’s account he had bought nearly 10 million shares by early 2005. He won election with Edward Bleier and Strauss Zelnick at the annual meeting on May 11, 2005.[^19][^15]

people.name: James W. Keyes
people.text: Former president and chief executive of 7-Eleven, appointed on July 2, 2007 at age 52. He led the company into Chapter 11 and was terminated when the sale to Dish closed on April 26, 2011.[^16][^11][^13]

people.name: Edward B. Stead
people.text: Spoke for the company at the 2005 annual meeting.[^15] In Marc Randolph’s account he is the executive who asked Netflix to name its price in 2000.[^18]

people.name: Reed Hastings and Marc Randolph
people.text: By Randolph’s account they offered Netflix to Blockbuster for $50M in September 2000.[^18]

people.name: Sandi Harding
people.text: Runs the last store for its owners, Ken and Debbie Tisher, and is the central figure of The Last Blockbuster.[^30]

blocks.body: Blockbuster tried to buy Hollywood Entertainment in early 2005, offering $11.50 in cash and $3.00 in stock per share. It let the offer expire on March 24, 2005, citing “the unlikely resolution of the Company’s request for regulatory clearance on an acceptable timetable.”[^5]

Hollywood Entertainment, the chain Blockbuster bid for, was profitable when the offer lapsed. Its FY2004 10-K reports restated net income of $71.3M on revenue of $1.78B for 2004, and long-term obligations, including the current portion, of $351.3M at the end of that year.[^44] Blockbuster’s own 2004 result is in The numbers.

notes.label: Editorial: the year of death
notes.text: We set the end of the original business at 2010, the year Blockbuster Inc. filed for Chapter 11 (September 23).[^11] The stores kept trading under Dish Network until January 2014, and a franchise still trades today, which is why the tier is ghost. The start year, 1985, is the first store; the predecessor company was incorporated in 1982.[^1]

notes.label: Derived
notes.text: Cumulative net loss, 1997–2010, of about $6.70B is the sum of the annual net losses less the one profitable year: 318.2 + 336.6 + 69.2 + 75.9 + 238.8 + 1,621.1 + 978.7 + 1,248.8 + 588.1 − 50.5 + 73.8 + 374.1 + 558.2 + 268.0 = $6,699.0M.[^2][^3][^6][^9][^10] Most of it is non-cash write-downs of goodwill. The $905.6M distribution divided by Netflix’s $50M asking price is 18.1.[^5][^18] The fall in stores from 9,094 to 5,335 is 41%.[^6][^10] The rise in long-term debt in 2004 is $1,119.7M − $75.1M = $1,044.6M.[^6] “25 countries” is the United States plus the 24 other countries in the FY2004 10-K.[^5] “Days from the first store to the filing” and similar intervals are counted from the cited dates.

notes.label: Basis changes in the filings
notes.text: Revenue for 1995–2005 is as reported in the FY1999, FY2000 and FY2005 10-Ks.[^2][^3][^6] Revenue for 2006–2009 is from the FY2009 10-K, which restated earlier years to remove discontinued operations (on that basis 2005 was $5,551.1M, against $5,864.4M as first reported).[^9] 2010 is from the FY2010 10-K.[^10] Long-term debt before 2001 is shown “less current portion”; from 2001 it is “including capital leases”.[^3][^6] Net loss for 2005 is $588.1M as first reported and $583.9M as restated.

notes.label: Estimates
notes.text: Blockbuster’s own projection, made in March 2005, was that late fees would have contributed $400M to $450M of revenue and $250M to $300M of operating income in 2005.[^5] It is a company estimate, not a reported result. The “nearly $1 billion” of debt at the filing is the company’s wording.[^11]

notes.label: Unverified
notes.text: The widely repeated figure of about $800M of late-fee income in 2000 is **unverified**: we could not find it in the FY2000 10-K. The last year for which we found the figure in a filing is 1999, at $692.6M.[^2] The account of the September 2000 meeting at which Netflix asked $50M is Marc Randolph’s, published in 2019; we found no Blockbuster filing or statement that confirms or disputes it.[^18] The airing years of the commercials come from the uploaders. We did not find the size of David Cook’s stake sale in 1987 or the price Wayne Huizenga’s group paid in a primary source, so neither is stated.

notes.label: Unknown
notes.text: The terms on which the Bend store uses the name are not public, and we found no current statement from Dish or EchoStar about its plans for the brand. EchoStar’s FY2025 10-K does not mention Blockbuster.[^36] The number of franchise stores open between 2014 and 2018 is known only from press counts.

notes.label: General knowledge
notes.text: Sling TV is a streaming service owned by Dish Network. The Last Blockbuster was first released in 2020. Chapter 11 is the reorganisation chapter of the U.S. Bankruptcy Code and Chapter 7 the liquidation chapter.

notes.label: Images
notes.text: Screenshots are of Internet Archive captures.[^33] Photographs are from Wikimedia Commons under the licenses given in the gallery credits. Drawings are original illustrations, not official assets.

notes.label: Derived: the store map
notes.text: Between the 2004 and 2009 state tables, franchised stores fell by more than half, (493 − 1,095) ÷ 1,095, and company-operated stores by about a quarter, (3,525 − 4,708) ÷ 4,708. All U.S. stores fell by about 31 percent, (4,018 − 5,803) ÷ 5,803. California lost the most stores, 681 − 468, and Montana the largest share, (8 − 1) ÷ 8. The inputs are the printed totals and state counts in the FY2004 and FY2009 10-Ks.[^5]

notes.label: Scope of the added charts
notes.text: The stock chart shows Class A high and low sale prices as printed in each year’s Form 10-K, not closing prices or total returns, and they are not adjusted for the special distribution of September 2004. The store counts for Blockbuster cover the United States and its territories, company-operated plus franchised, and exclude kiosks. Movie Gallery’s counts are consolidated totals that include Canada. Hollywood Video’s counts exclude Game Crazy departments. Dish’s counts after 2010 cover only the stores it operated and are not drawn on the chart.[^3][^5][^6][^37][^44][^45][^46]

notes.label: Not found
notes.text: We did not find how Blockbuster’s 2008 proposal for Circuit City ended.[^53] We did not find the date the bankruptcy case moved to Chapter 7; the CourtListener record is metadata, and its docket page did not open in our checks.[^52] Dish’s FY2013 10-K says Blockbuster had ceased all material operations as of December 31, 2013, and no source we found gives the date the last store closed.[^28] The Bend store’s own website could not be reached by script on October 10, 2026, so the latest report of the store we could read is Seattle Met’s.[^50] We found no source that names the parent of Blockbuster L.L.C. today.

story.title: Nine thousand stores, a billion of debt and a rival it would not buy
story.lede: Blockbuster did not lose its customers in a single season. It lost its profits first, then its balance sheet, and only then its stores.

chapters.title: A video store built like a supermarket
chapters.cap: value of the merger with Viacom announced on January 7, 1994
chapters.body:
The first Blockbuster opened in Dallas on October 19, 1985. Its founder, David Cook, had run a software business serving the Texas oil industry, and the store reflected it: some 8,000 tapes on open shelves and a computerized checkout, at a time when most video shops were small and thinly stocked.[^20] The predecessor company, Blockbuster Entertainment Corporation, had been incorporated in Delaware in 1982 and entered the rental business in 1985.[^1]

In 1987 Cook sold part of the business to a group of investors that included Wayne Huizenga, a founder of Waste Management. Cook left later that year, Huizenga took control and the headquarters moved to Fort Lauderdale. By 1988 the chain had some 400 stores and was the largest in the country.[^20] On January 7, 1994 Viacom and Blockbuster announced a merger valued at **$8.4 billion**; it closed on September 29, 1994.[^14][^1]

image.caption: A Blockbuster Video membership card. Via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.
image.alt: Blue and yellow Blockbuster Video membership card shaped like a torn ticket

chapters.title: “Make it a Blockbuster night”
chapters.cap: stores worldwide on December 31, 2004, the most it ever had
chapters.body:
Under Viacom the chain roughly doubled, from 4,513 stores at the end of 1995 to 9,094 at the end of 2004.[^2][^6] In 1998 it signed revenue-sharing agreements with the major studios. Until then it had paid between $60 and $70 for each rental cassette of a major release; afterwards it paid a small sum up front and shared the rental income, which let it fill the new-release wall.[^1]

Viacom sold a minority of the company to the public on August 10, 1999: 31 million shares at $15, raising $465 million.[^1][^2] It kept about 81.5%.[^4] Extended viewing fees, the company’s term for late fees, were **$692.6M** in 1999, or 15.5% of revenue.[^2]

chapters.title: The meeting in Dallas
chapters.cap: what Netflix asked for itself in September 2000, by Marc Randolph’s account
chapters.body:
In September 2000, according to Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph, he, Reed Hastings and Barry McCarthy flew to Dallas to propose that Blockbuster buy Netflix. Asked for a number, Hastings said fifty million. Randolph writes that John Antioco, Blockbuster’s chief executive, “was struggling not to laugh.”[^18] The account is Randolph’s; Blockbuster’s filings do not mention the meeting.

Blockbuster’s FY2003 annual report called Netflix “our primary domestic competitor in online rental” and warned that rental services with no late fees “could reduce the number of consumers who obtain product from our stores.”[^4] Blockbuster Online launched in August 2004.[^5] It had about 1.2 million subscribers at the end of 2005 and about 2.2 million at the end of 2006, after Total Access let customers swap mailed discs in stores.[^6][^7] Netflix had 6.3 million.[^21]
chapters.artCaption: A disc in a paper envelope: the format that made the drive to the store optional. Original illustration.

chapters.when: 2004 – 2007 · Debt, late fees and Carl Icahn
chapters.title: Independent, indebted and under new management
chapters.cap: rise in long-term debt during 2004, the year of the split from Viacom (derived)
chapters.body:
Viacom decided in February 2004 to divest its stake.[^4] Before the split-off was completed that October, Blockbuster took out a $1,150M credit facility, issued $300M of 9% notes and paid shareholders, chiefly Viacom, a special distribution of $5.00 a share, about **$905.6M**.[^5] Long-term debt rose from $75.1M at the end of 2003 to $1,119.7M a year later.[^6] The divestiture ran through an exchange offer in September 2004: Viacom offered its shareholders 5.15 Blockbuster shares for each Viacom share, the offer was oversubscribed, and Viacom accepted 9.55% of the tendered shares, 27,961,165 in all, in exchange for 72 million shares each of Blockbuster’s Class A and Class B stock.[^5]

On January 1, 2005 it stopped charging late fees at more than 4,500 company stores. Its own projection was that the fees would have brought in $400M to $450M of revenue and $250M to $300M of operating income that year.[^5] The FY2005 annual report measured the “no late fees” program itself: about $60 million in marketing and implementation costs in 2005 and a reduction of rental revenues by over $500 million, against extended viewing fees that had been approximately 14% of 2004 rental revenues.[^6] The two statements may not share a baseline, so we do not subtract one from the other. By March 1, 2006 about 340 franchise stores in the United States had also ended the fees.[^6] In May 2005 Carl Icahn and two allies were elected to the board, displacing Antioco as a director until the board reappointed him.[^15] After a dispute over his 2006 bonus, Antioco agreed to leave, and James Keyes, formerly of 7-Eleven, became chairman and chief executive on July 2, 2007.[^17][^16]

chapters.title: Chapter 11, then an auction
chapters.cap: paid by Dish Network for substantially all of the assets, April 26, 2011
chapters.body:
Revenue held above $5B through 2008, then fell to $4.06B in 2009 and $3.24B in 2010.[^9][^10] The company closed 374 U.S. company-owned stores in 2009, and its FY2009 annual report said that conditions “raise substantial doubt about our ability to continue as a going concern.”[^9] By then [Redbox](/redbox/) was running some 30,200 kiosks and Netflix had 20 million subscribers.[^24][^22]

On September 23, 2010 Blockbuster and its U.S. subsidiaries filed for Chapter 11 in New York, with a plan to cut debt “from nearly $1 billion currently to an estimated $100 million or less.”[^11] The plan did not hold. The assets went to auction on April 6, 2011, Dish Network won, and [the sale closed on April 26](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1085734/000119312511132032/d8k.htm) for **$320.6M**. Stockholders received nothing.[^12][^13]

Dish’s announcement of April 6, 2011 put its winning bid at approximately $320 million and said it expected to pay approximately $228 million in cash at closing, after adjustments for cash and inventory. Of the $320.6M Dish paid, the estate expected about $226 million in net proceeds.[^51][^13]

image.caption: A Blockbuster Video in Miami Beach during its closing sale, November 2013. Photo: Phillip Pessar, via Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.0.
image.alt: Blockbuster Video storefront in Miami Beach with a yellow Store Closing banner

chapters.title: One store in Oregon
chapters.cap: Blockbuster store left in the world, at 211 NE Revere Avenue, Bend, Oregon
chapters.body:
Dish’s own counts show the pace. Its announcement of April 6, 2011 described Blockbuster as having more than 1,700 store locations.[^51] On December 31, 2011 Blockbuster operated over 1,500 retail stores in the United States.[^39] During 2012 Dish closed approximately 700 domestic stores, leaving approximately 800, and in January 2013 it announced the closing of approximately 300 more.[^40] These are Dish’s counts of its own stores, in the rounded wording of its filings, and they are not comparable with the franchise-inclusive U.S. counts above. The 1,700 figure does not say which countries it covers.

Dish kept closing stores, and on November 6, 2013 it announced that the remaining 300 or so company-owned U.S. stores would shut by early January, along with the DVD-by-mail service. About 2,800 jobs went. About 50 franchised stores stayed open.[^27][^28]

They closed one by one. The two in Alaska shut in 2018 and the last overseas store, in Perth, Australia, in 2019, leaving a franchise in Bend, Oregon that had opened in 1992 as Pacific Video and become a Blockbuster in 2000.[^29][^30] A documentary about it, The Last Blockbuster, reached Netflix on March 15, 2021.[^30] [The store’s website](https://bendblockbuster.com/) was live when we checked on October 3, 2026, listing new releases for rent and a line of merchandise under the heading “The Lone Survivor.”[^31]

timeline.lede: From the predecessor’s incorporation to the one store still open, with the money and the rivals alongside. Filter by thread.

events.text: Extended viewing fees end at more than 4,500 company stores and about 550 franchise stores. Items kept past a one-week grace period are sold to the customer.

events.text: Blockbuster offers $14.50 a share for Hollywood Entertainment. It lets the offer expire on March 24, citing antitrust clearance.

events.text: Online subscribers can return mailed DVDs to a store and take a free rental, and subscribers pass 2 million by year-end.

events.text: The former chief executive of 7-Eleven is named chairman and chief executive.

events.text: An agreement to put Blockbuster-branded vending kiosks in retail locations. There were 2,225 by January 2010.

events.title: Offer for Circuit City
events.text: Blockbuster makes public an offer, sent in a letter on February 17, to buy [Circuit City](/circuit-city/) for at least $6.00 a share in cash, subject to due diligence. We did not find how the proposal ended.

events.text: The FY2009 annual report cites “substantial doubt” about the company’s ability to continue. It closed 374 U.S. stores in 2009.

events.title: About 800 stores left
events.text: Dish closed approximately 700 domestic stores during 2012. In January 2013 it announced the closing of approximately 300 more.

events.title: Blockbuster UK enters administration
events.text: The two UK operating subsidiaries enter administration. Dish’s Form 8-K reports a $21 million charge for writing down the assets and expects a further $25 million impairment on intercompany receivables. Its FY2013 10-K puts the total at approximately $46 million before tax.

events.text: The last 300 or so company-owned U.S. stores and the by-mail service are to shut by early January 2014.

events.text: Engadget reports that all 91 remaining UK stores are to close on December 16, with 808 employees losing their jobs.

events.text: Dish completes the sale of Blockbuster Mexico, after recording pre-tax impairment charges of $19 million in 2013.

events.title: Bend alone in the lower 48

whatif.title: What if…

forks.actual: By Marc Randolph’s account, Netflix offered itself to Blockbuster for $50M in September 2000 and was turned down.[^18] Blockbuster launched its own online service in August 2004.[^5] By the end of 2006 it had about 2.2 million online subscribers to Netflix’s 6.3 million.[^7][^21]
forks.whatif: A purchase would have given Blockbuster a four-year head start by mail. It would not have guaranteed the rest. Netflix inside Blockbuster would have answered to a company that earned $692.6M a year from late fees[^2], and the subscription model’s selling point was that it had none. The likelier outcome is a smaller Netflix and no surviving Blockbuster.

forks.actual: Before the 2004 split-off Blockbuster borrowed under a $1,150M facility, issued $300M of notes and paid a $905.6M special distribution. Long-term debt ended the year at $1,119.7M.[^5][^6]
forks.whatif: Without the distribution the company would have entered 2005 nearly debt-free, with room to fund Blockbuster Online and absorb the loss of late fees at the same time. It was losing customers either way, but the 2010 filing was a balance-sheet event: the plan’s stated purpose was to cut debt from nearly $1 billion to $100 million or less.[^11]

forks.actual: Total Access launched on November 1, 2006 and took online subscribers past 2 million within two months.[^7] John Antioco, who had backed it, agreed in March 2007 to leave, and James Keyes replaced him that July.[^17][^16] Antioco later wrote about the disagreement with Carl Icahn’s board.[^19]
forks.whatif: The offer of free in-store exchanges was something Netflix could not copy, and it was expensive for the same reason. Kept at full strength it might have held more subscribers into the streaming years. Whether a company with a billion dollars of debt could have afforded to keep paying for it is the open question.

whatif.method: Each fork starts from a documented decision and cites it in the actual column. The what-if column is speculation by the Spectre Brands editors and is not a measured outcome.

context.title: The meeting in Dallas
context.cap: what Netflix asked for itself in September 2000, by Marc Randolph’s account
context.body:
In September 2000, according to Netflix co-founder Marc Randolph, he, Reed Hastings and Barry McCarthy flew to Dallas to propose that Blockbuster buy Netflix. Asked for a number, Hastings said fifty million. Randolph writes that John Antioco, Blockbuster’s chief executive, “was struggling not to laugh.”[^18] The account is Randolph’s; Blockbuster’s filings do not mention the meeting.

Blockbuster’s FY2003 annual report called Netflix “our primary domestic competitor in online rental” and warned that rental services with no late fees “could reduce the number of consumers who obtain product from our stores.”[^4] Blockbuster Online launched in August 2004.[^5] It had about 1.2 million subscribers at the end of 2005 and about 2.2 million at the end of 2006, after Total Access let customers swap mailed discs in stores.[^6][^7] Netflix had 6.3 million.[^21]

now.title: The sock puppet
now.text: In March 2000 Pets.com signed an exclusive representation agreement with Brian P. Hakan & Associates, Inc. On Jun 12, 2002 it sued Fun-4-All Corporation, one of the licensees, for $152,567 of past-due royalties; Fun-4-All cross-complained for damages “in excess of $250,000.” The filings do not say whether the two Hakan companies are the same, and we found no record of who holds the rights now.

blocks.title: Heavy, cheap, bulky
blocks.caption: Original drawing, not an official Pets.com asset.
blocks.body:
Litter and kibble are cheap to buy and expensive to ship. The prospectus put shipping at 100–110% of revenue in late 1999 and listed “shipping below our actual costs” as a risk.[^1] In the filings, cost of goods sold includes outbound shipping, and it ran above net sales in every quarter reported.[^2][^4]

We don’t repeat the widely told 40-lb-bag anecdotes: [we found no order-level data behind them](/about/#honesty).

blocks.title: What the gross margin counted
blocks.body:
Pets.com’s prospectus put fulfillment expenses in marketing and sales, not in cost of sales, which it defined as the cost of products plus outbound and inbound shipping.[^1] The Q3 2000 10-Q still lists distribution expenses and distribution payroll under marketing and sales.[^4] The gross margin that improved through 2000 therefore never carried the cost of picking and packing a box. Only the marketing view of the chart above does.

Pets.com did not disclose that cost in dollars. Its Petstore.com deal does show one rival’s. In a pro forma filing, Pets.com moved $2,959K of Petstore.com’s 1999 cost of goods sold, which was $5,161K as reported, into marketing and sales to match its own classification.[^48] Petstore.com’s net sales that year were 2,100,462 dollars, so the fulfillment cost alone was larger than its sales.[^48] For the first half of 2000 the move was $3,974K out of $10,163K, nearly as much as that half-year’s net sales.[^48]

Other delivery companies drew the line elsewhere. Kozmo booked delivery, mostly payroll for its delivery staff, as an operating expense below gross profit.[^50] PetSmart.com defined its cost of net revenues as products, promotional products and shipping.[^44] Headline gross margins from the four are not like-for-like, and we found no filing in which Pets.com changed its own classification.

The prospectus put shipping at **100–110% of revenue**[^1], before the cost of the food itself. Gross margin was **−64%** in Q1 2000 and **−20%** in Q2. It only reached **−3%** in Q3, “as our second distribution center in Indianapolis reached its full load.”[^4] When PETsMART.com took over the customers, its coupon excluded dog food, cat food and litter from the $25 minimum.[^36]

We found no primary source for the often-repeated story of a specific 40-lb bag sold at a set loss, so we don’t print one.

blocks.body: The same idea, a decade later. Chewy (founded 2011) built on subscriptions (Autoship) and positive gross margins.

blocks.title: Scheduled delivery was already common
blocks.body:
Subscriptions did not separate the rivals. Pets.com’s prospectus described Keep It Comin’, which let customers schedule ongoing deliveries of food and litter.[^1] PetSmart.com’s S-1 described an automatic replenishment service, You Sit, We Fetch.[^44] Petopia said a significant portion of its revenue came from its replenishment subscription service, the Bottomless Bowl.[^46]

What the filings do show is how the first years differed. PetSmart.com sold more than Pets.com, spent less on marketing and sales, and still lost $47.495M. Substantially all of its sales were fulfilled by its partner PetSmart.[^44] On Dec 20, 2000 PetSmart took control of the unit.[^58]

story.title: A sock puppet, a Super Bowl and negative gross margins
story.lede: Pets.com didn’t die because nobody had heard of it. Everybody had. It died because every box it shipped lost money, and the cash ran out before that changed.

chapters.title: An Amazon-backed bet on the pet aisle
chapters.cap: raised privately in 1999 across three preferred stock rounds
chapters.body:
Pets.com was incorporated in California on October 7, 1998. It began operating on February 17, 1999, when it bought the Pets.com domain and a web store from a third party.[^1] An archived page from May 1999 still described the site as “a division of WebMagic™… headed by Greg McLemore.”[^36] Julie Wainwright, who had just been CEO of Reel.com, took over as CEO in March 1999.[^1]

Money arrived fast: a $10.0M Series A in April, a $50.0M Series B in June and another $49.2M in November–December.[^1] Just before the IPO, Amazon.com owned **40.7%** of the company and Hummer Winblad Venture Partners 21.2%.[^1] Headcount went from 4 people in March 1999 to 270 by December.[^1]

The address was older than the company. The .com registry shows pets.com was first registered on Nov 21, 1994, almost four years before Pets.com, Inc. was incorporated.[^54]

chapters.title: The mascot that outlived the company
chapters.cap: spent on marketing & sales for every $1 of revenue in Q4 1999
chapters.body:
TBWA\Chiat\Day[^16] created a wisecracking sock puppet, performed by comedian Michael Ian Black.[^13] It floated as a 36-foot balloon in the 1999 Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade[^13], did Good Morning America and Time[^14], and on January 30, 2000 got its own Super Bowl XXXIV spot, a buy widely reported at about $1.2 million.[^16]

Advertising expense alone was **$26.9M** from inception to December 31, 1999[^1]. In Q4 1999, marketing & sales was **$30.7M** against **$5.2M** in net sales.[^2]

chapters.title: Public, four weeks before the top
chapters.cap: IPO price on Feb 11, 2000 (Nasdaq: IPET). The high for the quarter was $14.00
chapters.body:
Merrill Lynch led the sale of 7.5 million shares at $11, raising $82.5M gross and about $75.3M net.[^6] The stock opened at $13½ and was back near $11 by midday. CNET’s headline was “Pets.com IPO is a dog.”[^12]

On March 10 the Nasdaq closed at its all-time bubble high.[^26] [The prospectus](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/1100683/000089161800000749/0000891618-00-000749.txt) had already warned that the company might “provide our customers with shipping below our actual costs to attract customers.”[^1]

The offering closed on Feb 16, 2000. Merrill Lynch, Bear Stearns, Thomas Weisel Partners and Warburg Dillon Read were the managing underwriters.[^40]

chapters.title: “Fewer than 8 were even prepared to visit”
chapters.cap: closing price on Nov 7, 2000, down 98% from the IPO price
chapters.body:
Cutting marketing narrowed the losses, from $39.1M in Q1 2000 to $21.7M in Q3. Gross margin improved from −64% to −3% once the Indianapolis-area warehouse took over its share of shipping.[^4] But by September 30 only $23.1M in cash was left.[^4] In July it absorbed rival Petstore.com in an all-stock deal that brought in just $3M of cash.[^7]

Petstore.com, a majority-owned subsidiary of Discovery Communications, was the rival it bought.[^48] Pets.com paid 5,243,752 common shares for its brand, website, customer base, live fish business, supplier agreements and intellectual property, valued at $10.3 million.[^43] The filing priced those shares at $1.8125, the Jul 12 close.[^48] Alongside the deal Discovery bought $3 million of Series A redeemable preferred stock and common stock from Pets.com.[^6]

Merrill Lynch approached more than 50 potential buyers and investors. “Out of the more than 50 prospects contacted, fewer than 8 were even prepared to visit with the company.”[^5] On November 7, 2000, about 255 of the 320 employees were laid off.[^5]

chapters.title: Sold for parts
chapters.cap: total liquidation payout per share, 2001–2004, on an $11 IPO price
chapters.body:
The site stopped taking orders at 11am Pacific on November 9, 2000.[^36] PetSmart.com paid **$375,000** for the domain names and related IP. The sock puppet was explicitly excluded from the deal.[^6] In its December proxy, the board estimated stockholders might receive “up to approximately $0.25 per share.”[^24]

They got less. Three liquidating distributions followed: $0.09 in 2001, $0.075 in 2002 and a final $0.00747 in 2004.[^8][^9][^10]

The estate’s own statements show how fast the books shrank. Net assets in liquidation were $58.7M when liquidation accounting began, $9.6M at Dec 31, 2000 and $4.2M a year later.[^40] Most of the first drop was write-offs: $45.8M of net other expense in the first eight weeks, which included recovering 5,243,752 shares in settlement of an advertising and cross-marketing agreement.[^40] The first two payouts are on the record as paid: $3,128,127 on Sep 28, 2001 and, in September 2002, $2,605,581.[^40][^41]

whatif.title: What if…

forks.actual: Pets.com sold products below their delivered cost. Cost of goods sold, which by the company’s definition includes outbound and inbound shipping, ran above net sales every quarter, peaking at a −211% gross margin in Q3 1999.[^4] The prospectus acknowledged it might offer “shipping below our actual costs to attract customers.”[^1]
forks.whatif: Pricing heavy, low-margin goods like litter and kibble at or above landed cost, or adding a shipping threshold, would have meant slower growth but positive unit economics. By Q3 2000 the gross margin was −3%, almost break-even.[^4] Getting there a year earlier might have stretched the runway past the 2000 funding freeze.

forks.actual: Marketing and sales spend hit $30.7M in Q4 1999 and $28.9M in Q1 2000, the Super Bowl quarter, while quarterly sales were $5.2M and $7.7M.[^2] eCompany Now, citing PC Data Online, reported that site traffic actually fell the month after the Super Bowl ad.[^15]
forks.whatif: Spending in channels aimed at pet owners (vets, plus the Amazon cross-promotion it already had[^1]) instead of mass-market TV could have kept tens of millions in the bank. That would have been enough to cover the roughly $20M an analyst said it needed to keep going.[^11]

forks.actual: Four VC-funded online pet stores fought each other on price (see Section 08). Pets.com didn’t absorb Petstore.com until July 2000[^7], after the IPO window had closed.
forks.whatif: A merger in 1999, while private capital was still plentiful, could have removed a price war and combined marketing budgets. Chewy’s later dominance suggests the category could support one well-run leader, but probably not four money-losing ones.

whatif.method: The first column of each fork cites filings. The what-if column is our speculation, and none of it is modeled from order-level data, which we did not find.

company.description: Orbitz was a fruit drink with floating gel balls from Clearly Canadian. It was a hit in 1997, its sales fell almost 85% in early 1998 and it was gone by 1999.

card.blurb: Clearly Canadian’s 1996 drink with colored gel balls suspended in fruit-flavored water. It was a sensation with teenagers for a year; first-half sales fell from $9.4M in 1997 to $1.46M in 1998, and the company stopped making it.

hero.standfirst: A drink you could chew. Teenagers tried it once.
hero.deck: Orbitz was a [non-carbonated fruit drink](/category/consumer/) from Clearly Canadian, the Vancouver maker of flavored sparkling waters, and it had been discontinued by 1999. Its selling point was the small balls of gellan gum that hung, without sinking, in the liquid. Launched in 1996 for 12- to 17-year-olds, it sold a million cases in its first months, by the company’s account, and was a hit in 1997. In the first half of 1998 its sales fell by almost 85%. The company said this was the life cycle it had expected; by 1999 the drink was gone. It rests on [contemporary press and Clearly Canadian’s own SEC filings](#sources).

findings.title: Built to be talked about, not repeated.
findings.text: Its spokesman said the aim was to make whoever brought Orbitz into a room “the center of attention for a few moments.”[^1] Reviewers called it a lava lamp, tapioca and worse.[^1][^2]

findings.title: The collapse was in the plan.
findings.text: When first-half sales fell from $9.4M to $1.46M, the marketing chief said: “Our expected life-cycle of the product is coming true.”[^4]

findings.title: No advertising budget to rescue it.
findings.text: Clearly Canadian relied on product placement, sampling and events, saying advertising was “too mass for our products and, quite frankly, not affordable.”[^4]

findings.title: The parent kept shrinking.
findings.text: Clearly Canadian’s revenue fell from $34.9M in 1998 to $20.5M in 2002, with losses in every year after 1998. Its own filings warned that beverage brands may last “a few years” before tastes change.[^6]

factFile.value: A non-carbonated fruit drink with floating gel spheres, made by Clearly Canadian Beverage Corporation of Vancouver

factFile.label: Launched
factFile.value: Introduced in the United States in May 1996, according to Science World in October 1996; the Canadian launch was announced on April 14, 1997, with sales from May 1, 1997

Discontinued by 1999 (Gastro Obscura). A company-history reference says sales were suspended, with a significant writedown, in its account of the fall of 1999; no primary source gives a date.

None: Orbitz was a product, not a company. Its maker filed a proposal to its creditors under Canada’s Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act on March 17, 2010. Fast Company reported in October 2024 that Robert R. Khan acquired the Clearly Canadian company in 2012.

No current owner found. The maker’s 2006 application for ORBITZ was abandoned in December 2008, and a 2014 application by a different applicant was abandoned on request. Fast Company reported in October 2024 that the old owners sold the trademark; it did not name a buyer.

Unopened bottles for collectors: Gastro Obscura says one can sell for around $50 on eBay. Fast Company reported that the machine that made the spheres was sold for parts, and that Clearly Canadian itself resumed full-scale production in 2017.

items.title: The drink
items.text: Not made since about 1999; Clearly Canadian said in 2015 that it lacked the equipment.[^5]

items.title: The bottles
items.text: Unopened bottles from the 1990s sell for around $50 on eBay.[^5]

items.title: The maker
items.text: Clearly Canadian still sells its sparkling water under its own name. Its online shop showed only a “nearly ready” notice when we loaded it in October 2026.[^7]

items.title: The name
items.text: The maker applied to register ORBITZ in September 2006, and the application was abandoned in December 2008 for want of a statement of use or extension request.[^22] A different applicant filed ORBITZ DEFY GRAVITY DRINK ORBITZ on March 5, 2014 and abandoned it on request on May 9, 2014, about two months later.[^23] Fast Company reported in October 2024 that the old owners had sold the trademark, without naming a buyer.[^24] The records we opened do not name a current owner of any ORBITZ beverage mark.

items.title: The machine
items.text: The machine that made the spheres broke down and was sold off for parts, Fast Company reported in October 2024.[^24]

items.title: The address
items.text: The drink’s Planet Orbitz site ran at orbitz.com. The address was on the packaging in April 1997,[^8] archive captures show the Orbiterium prelude in December 1997 and January 1999, and by February 2000 the address showed a domain-service placeholder. By January 2001 it carried ©2000 Orbitz, LLC, and by May 2001 a travel search preview.[^35] Our sources do not say how the address changed hands or who holds it today.

items.title: The maker, 2010 to 2017
items.text: Clearly Canadian Beverage Corporation filed a proposal to its creditors under Canada’s Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act on March 17, 2010.[^27] Creditors approved it on April 1 and the Supreme Court of British Columbia on April 26.[^28][^29] The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission revoked the registrations of each class of its registered securities on January 4, 2017.[^31]

items.title: The Clearly Canadian brand
items.text: Fast Company reported in October 2024 that production stopped around 2010, that Robert R. Khan acquired the company in 2012 and that full-scale production resumed in 2017. It said a group of private investors who were fans of the brand from the ’90s owned it, and its marketing chief said the company was on track to sell around 45 million bottles that year.[^24]

now.title: The drink
now.text: Not made. In 2015 a company representative said it lacked the equipment; in October 2024 Clearly Canadian’s marketing chief said the machine that made the spheres broke down and was sold off for parts.

now.title: The name
now.text: The maker’s 2006 application for ORBITZ was abandoned in December 2008, and an unrelated 2014 application was withdrawn within two months. Fast Company says the old owners sold the trademark; the buyer is not named and we could not find a live ORBITZ beverage registration.

now.title: The maker, 2010 to 2017
now.text: Clearly Canadian Beverage Corporation filed a creditor proposal on Mar 17, 2010. Its creditors approved it on Apr 1, 2010 and the Supreme Court of British Columbia on Apr 26, 2010. The SEC [revoked the registration of its securities](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/808464/999999999717000011/filename1.pdf) on Jan 4, 2017.

now.title: The Clearly Canadian brand
now.text: Acquired in 2012 by Robert R. Khan, back in full production in 2017 and, as of October 2024, owned by a group of private investors. Clearly Canadian said it was on track to sell about 45 million bottles in 2024.

now.title: orbitz.com
now.text: The drink’s Planet Orbitz site was at orbitz.com. The address was on the packaging in April 1997, and archive captures show the Orbiterium prelude in December 1997 and January 1999. By February 2000 the address was a parked page, and by January 2001 it carried the airline-backed Orbitz, LLC. No source we could open says how the address changed hands.

now.title: The bottles
now.text: An unopened, decades-old bottle sells for around $50 on eBay, according to Gastro Obscura (undated).

now.title: The people
now.text: Douglas Mason, who founded Clearly Canadian and led it as chief executive, was replaced in that role in October 2005 when Brent Lokash became president. Jonathan Cronin, the marketing executive quoted on Orbitz, moved to the US subsidiary in December 1998.

cause.title: The autopsy

causes.title: A novelty, by design
causes.text: The company built Orbitz to be talked about and expected sales to fade: “Our expected life-cycle of the product is coming true.”[^1][^4]

causes.title: People did not like drinking it
causes.text: Adult tasters gave it two stars; an AP office poll found two thumbs up among more than a dozen.[^1][^2] One panelist wrote: “I don’t like any soft drink I have to chew.”[^2]

causes.title: No money to market it
causes.text: Clearly Canadian did not advertise its niche brands, calling advertising “quite frankly, not affordable.”[^4]

causes.title: Shelf space and distribution
causes.text: The company’s filings describe independent distributors being absorbed by the big soft-drink companies and becoming less willing to carry other makers’ new-age drinks.[^6]

story.title: Planet Orbitz
story.lede: Orbitz was designed as a novelty and sold like one: fast, then not at all.

chapters.title: “A lava lamp you can drink”
chapters.cap: cases sold by the end of 1996, by the company’s account
chapters.body:
Clearly Canadian, then nine years old and known for flavored sparkling water, launched Orbitz in 1996.[^1][^4] It used “fluid-gel” technology to keep small balls of gellan gum suspended in non-carbonated fruit drink, in flavors such as raspberry citrus and blueberry melon strawberry.[^1] The company aimed it at 12- to 17-year-olds and talked about a “Jetsons mentality.”[^1]

The Associated Press called it “a lava lamp you can drink” and, less kindly, “fruit-flavored phlegm in a bottle.” A product consultant called it potentially “the pet rock of the beverage industry.”[^1] The company reported better-than-expected sales: a million cases by the end of the year.[^1]

Science World reported that October that Orbitz had been introduced around the country the previous May.[^9] By July 24, 1996 a University of Arizona summer newspaper had listed it among the summer’s test-market launches, a non-carbonated, fruit-flavored drink with colorful floating spheres.[^11]

The press treated it as a stunt. Katie Couric tried it on NBC’s Today; her first reaction, by AP’s account, was “Ugh. Why?” and she later pronounced it a little interesting.[^1] BevNET, an early web beverage-review site, called it “just the strangest thing we have ever seen” in a review quoted by AP, and the marketing analyst Al Ries said beverage makers were getting desperate.[^1]

chapters.title: A liquid that holds a bead up
chapters.cap: yield stress of the liquid, measured by Minnesota rheologists
chapters.body:
Floating a gel ball in a drink is harder than it sounds. A patent application that Bush Boake Allen Inc. filed on October 25, 1995, titled Method of suspending inclusions, starts from the problem. Solid pieces in a beverage tend to sink to the bottom or float to the top, it says, especially when they are larger than about one cubic millimeter.[^12] The sources we opened do not say whether that patent covers Orbitz.

Jesse Wolff, a chemical engineer who helped develop Orbitz, told Science World that the liquid was what scientists call a fluid gel, made from ingredients similar to those in Jell-O.[^9] The magazine left a bottle alone for a few days. The spheres moved gradually down through the liquid but never sank to the bottom, and William Chalupa, a fluid-gel expert, conceded that gravity does indeed act on Orbitz.[^9] Shaking the bottle spread the matrix particles out and the spheres suspended again.[^9] A William F. Chalupa is also named as an inventor on the patent; we could not confirm that the two are one person.[^9][^12]

Rheologists put numbers on it. In August 1997 two participants in a University of Minnesota short course asked the instructors how gel-like particles, some as large as 5 mm across, stay suspended in the commercially available drink.[^10] P. Dontula and C. W. Macosko answered in the January 1999 issue of the Rheology Bulletin. Creep measurements gave the liquid a yield stress of 0.04 Pa, close to the 0.045 Pa from oscillatory tests and about twice what is used to suspend insoluble builder particles in liquid detergents.[^10] At a shear rate of 100 per second its viscosity was only four times that of water, which explains why it looks fluid at first sight. For particles 5 mm across, the largest density difference the liquid can support is about 12 kg/m3.[^10]

The paper adds that the liquid appears to have the consistency of water even though the suspension is stable to violent agitation.[^10] The authors used the measurements as a home exercise in a course, and learned that another professor had used the sample as a teaching example at the University of Michigan.[^10]
chapters.artCaption: Original illustration of a gel ball held in a liquid by a web of fine strands. Not to scale; not an official Orbitz asset.

chapters.title: Hot with teenagers, panned by adults
chapters.cap: Orbitz sales in the first half of 1997
chapters.body:
By 1997 it came in four flavors and sold for about $1.09 for a 10.14-ounce bottle, at 130 calories. The Spokesman-Review’s adult tasting panel gave it two stars; the only higher score came from a 13-year-old.[^2] The Washington Post reported that Orbitz had “captured a niche market among young people.”[^3]

Sales in the first half of 1997 were $9.4M.[^4]

Canada followed. On April 14, 1997 Clearly Canadian announced the Canadian launch of what it called North America’s first “texturally enhanced” alternative beverage, with sales from May 1 at accounts such as 7-Eleven, Shoppers Drug Mart and Famous Players cinemas.[^8] The campaign theme was “Defy Gravity. Get into Orbitz.”[^8] In the Washington region the exclusive distributor, Atlantic Beverage Co., had carried Orbitz for six weeks. Its president, Bill O’Leary, said Orbitz was “moving very well” after that time. To handle the added work, the company had moved its beverage operations to a Jessup plant nearly double the size of its old distribution site.[^3]

Douglas Mason, then president and chief executive, called the consumer response to the U.S. launch “overwhelmingly positive” and said the company planned to extend Orbitz to the United Kingdom, Australia, Sweden and selected Asian countries in 1997.[^8]

chapters.title: “Orbitz is still weird. It’s just not new.”
chapters.body:
In the first half of 1998 Orbitz sales were $1.46M. Clearly Canadian’s vice-president of marketing, Jonathan Cronin, said: “Orbitz is still weird. It’s just not new in 1998. We weren’t expecting Orbitz to sell in 1998 what it sold in 1997.”[^4] The company had no immediate plan to discontinue it, and moved on to an energy drink and an oxygenated water.[^4]

By 1999 Orbitz had been discontinued.[^5]

The rest of the record on the decline is thin and partly secondary. Strategy reported that, despite what it called feeble Orbitz sales, the company’s overall net profitability was improving.[^4] A company-history reference says a patent suit that Bush Boake Allen, which had supplied raw materials for Orbitz, brought against Clearly Canadian was settled in May 1998 with a licensing fee. It dates a buyback of distribution rights in several key Mid-Atlantic states to June 1998, and says sales of Orbitz were suspended, with a significant writedown, in its account of the fall of 1999.[^13] We found no court record of the suit, and no primary source gives the date Orbitz production ended.

The maker’s later annual reports put the decline in context. The U.S. new age beverage market grew from $3.8B in wholesale dollar sales in 1992 to an estimated $13.1B in 2002, Clearly Canadian’s [annual report for 2002](https://www.sec.gov/Archives/edgar/data/808464/000091228203000288/cc20f_2002.htm) said, citing Beverage Marketing Corporation, while the company’s own revenue fell.[^6] The same report warned that the lifecycle of a beverage brand may be limited to a few years in a distribution area, and that distribution companies once independent of the traditional soft-drink makers were less willing to distribute other companies’ new age beverages.[^6] Its Competition section names Hansen Natural Corp., a producer of natural sodas, smoothies, functional drinks, juices and iced teas.[^6] Hansen’s own annual report for 2002 shows net sales that rose in every year from 1998 to 2002.[^20]

chapters.title: From Planet Orbitz to Orbitz, LLC
chapters.cap: orbitz.com shows a domain-service placeholder, between the drink’s site and the travel company’s
chapters.body:
The drink had its own corner of the early web. The April 1997 Canadian release said the address of the Planet Orbitz site, www.orbitz.com, was prominently displayed on all Orbitz packaging, and described comics by the syndicated artist Dirk Van Stralen and a tour of an Orbiterium spaceship.[^8] A capture saved by the Internet Archive in December 1997 is a prelude page that invites visitors to set gravity aside and tour the Orbiterium, with one route for Netscape and another for Internet Explorer; a capture from January 1999 shows the same prelude.[^35]

By February 2000 the address showed a domain-service placeholder saying the domain was registered by a member of myinternet.com.[^35] The airline-backed travel venture, announced in November 1999 as T2 and incorporated on February 24, 2000 as DUNC, LLC, was officially named Orbitz, LLC and Orbitz, Inc. in July 2000, according to a company-history reference.[^14] A capture from January 2001 says that soon the difference will be clear, beside a notice of ©2000 Orbitz, LLC, and by May 2001 the page advertised a search of all airlines and over 2 billion fares.[^35]

No source we opened says how or when the address passed from the drink to the travel company, or whether Clearly Canadian sold it. The captures cited here show the before and the after; the change itself is not documented.

chapters.title: Collectors’ bottles
chapters.cap: about what an unopened 1990s bottle can fetch on eBay
chapters.body:
Clearly Canadian’s total revenue fell from $34.9M in 1998 to $20.5M in 2002, and it lost money every year from 1999 to 2002.[^6] In 2015 a company representative said fans still asked for Orbitz constantly, but that it no longer had the equipment to make it.[^5]

Unopened bottles from the 1990s sell to collectors for around $50.[^5] The balls do not always stay up: in a 2012 photograph of an old bottle they have sunk to the bottom.

The name outlived the drink on paper. The maker’s annual report for 2005 still cited Orbitz among the innovative products it could draw on, and its report for 2006 listed Orbitz among the products it had historically introduced.[^17][^18] In a November 2005 press release the company described Orbitz in the past tense, as a drink with gel spheres that seemed to defy gravity.[^26] On September 29, 2006 it applied to register ORBITZ with the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office for soft drinks, non-carbonated fruit-flavored beverages and energy drinks. The office published the application on February 12, 2008 and issued a notice of allowance on May 6, 2008; in December 2008 it recorded the application as abandoned because no statement of use or extension request was filed in time.[^22] A different applicant, an individual, filed ORBITZ DEFY GRAVITY DRINK ORBITZ for beverages on March 5, 2014 and abandoned it on request on May 9, 2014.[^23]

Fast Company reported in October 2024 that the old owners sold the trademark and that the machine that made the Orbitz spheres broke down and was sold off for parts; it did not name a buyer.[^24] Clearly Canadian itself came back, by the same article’s account: production stopped around 2010, Robert R. Khan acquired the company in 2012 and full-scale production resumed in 2017.[^24]

whatif.title: What if…

forks.actual: Orbitz targeted 12- to 17-year-olds and a “Jetsons mentality.”[^1]
forks.whatif: Bubble tea later made chewable drinks normal for adults. A version sold as a café drink rather than a teen novelty might have lasted longer. That is hindsight.

forks.actual: In 2015 the company said it no longer had the equipment to make Orbitz, despite steady requests.[^5]
forks.whatif: Keeping a small production line could have allowed occasional nostalgia runs, as [Crystal Pepsi](/crystal-pepsi/) and [Zima](/zima/) have done. Whether demand would cover the cost is unknown.

forks.actual: The maker applied to register ORBITZ in September 2006. The office issued a notice of allowance on May 6, 2008 and recorded the application as abandoned in December 2008, with neither a statement of use nor an extension request on file.[^22]
forks.whatif: A statement of use, or an extension request, would have kept the application alive. A registered ORBITZ might have been an asset to sell or revive when the company went to its creditors in 2010, or it might have changed nothing: the record does not show that anyone wanted to make the drink again.

forks.actual: By February 2000 orbitz.com showed a domain-service placeholder, and by January 2001 it carried a notice of ©2000 Orbitz, LLC.[^35] No source we opened says how the address changed hands.
forks.whatif: A drink maker that kept the address could have kept a home for fans of a discontinued drink. Whether Clearly Canadian sold the address, lost it or let it lapse is not documented, so the cost of keeping it cannot be priced.

whatif.method: These forks start from documented decisions and end where the record stops. They are our speculation, not findings.

context.title: A liquid that holds a bead up
context.cap: yield stress of the liquid, measured by Minnesota rheologists
context.body:
Floating a gel ball in a drink is harder than it sounds. A patent application that Bush Boake Allen Inc. filed on October 25, 1995, titled Method of suspending inclusions, starts from the problem. Solid pieces in a beverage tend to sink to the bottom or float to the top, it says, especially when they are larger than about one cubic millimeter.[^12] The sources we opened do not say whether that patent covers Orbitz.

Jesse Wolff, a chemical engineer who helped develop Orbitz, told Science World that the liquid was what scientists call a fluid gel, made from ingredients similar to those in Jell-O.[^9] The magazine left a bottle alone for a few days. The spheres moved gradually down through the liquid but never sank to the bottom, and William Chalupa, a fluid-gel expert, conceded that gravity does indeed act on Orbitz.[^9] Shaking the bottle spread the matrix particles out and the spheres suspended again.[^9] A William F. Chalupa is also named as an inventor on the patent; we could not confirm that the two are one person.[^9][^12]

Rheologists put numbers on it. In August 1997 two participants in a University of Minnesota short course asked the instructors how gel-like particles, some as large as 5 mm across, stay suspended in the commercially available drink.[^10] P. Dontula and C. W. Macosko answered in the January 1999 issue of the Rheology Bulletin. Creep measurements gave the liquid a yield stress of 0.04 Pa, close to the 0.045 Pa from oscillatory tests and about twice what is used to suspend insoluble builder particles in liquid detergents.[^10] At a shear rate of 100 per second its viscosity was only four times that of water, which explains why it looks fluid at first sight. For particles 5 mm across, the largest density difference the liquid can support is about 12 kg/m3.[^10]

The paper adds that the liquid appears to have the consistency of water even though the suspension is stable to violent agitation.[^10] The authors used the measurements as a home exercise in a course, and learned that another professor had used the sample as a teaching example at the University of Michigan.[^10]

points.text: The report for 2002 prints 20.477. The report for 2003 restates 2002 to 20.205 for discontinued operations.[^6][^15]

Revenue rose to 10.263 from 7.462. The company bought DMR Food Corporation, a snack maker, in February 2007, so the total is not a drink figure.[^19][^34]
